claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1–4, build a paired activation dataset for successful jailbreaks. Run open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on harmful requests from the public HarmBench and JailbreakBench datasets, both without an attack and with public attack templates from JailbreakBench; add benign and borderline examples from PKU-Alignment/BeaverTails and WildGuardMix. Retain matched cases in which the original request is refused but the attacked version is judged compliant by both a public HarmBench evaluator and blinded human review. Record every head output, attention pattern, residual-stream state, and next-token refusal/compliance logits at matched semantic positions. Test whether successful attacks produce concentrated reductions in the activation norms or safety-token logit contributions of a small number of heads, while harmfulness information remains decodable elsewhere using a preregistered zero-shot harmful-versus-benign verbalizer score. Concentrated suppression with persistent harmfulness signals would support bypass; disappearance of harmfulness signals throughout the network would support elimination; diffuse changes would reject the selective-head account. This observational screen identifies candidates but cannot establish causality, so it informs the following interventions.

To address subclaims 3 and 4, causally test whether successful jailbreaks bypass refusal by suppressing a small head set. On the matched cases from Experiment 1, use head-level path patching between the refused and successfully attacked runs: patch each attacked head output with its refusal-run counterpart and perform the reverse patch, initially one head at a time and then with sparse combinations. Validate that the relevant difference is suppression by continuously scaling each candidate head from its attacked activation toward its refusal activation, rather than relying only on zero ablation. Preregister ‘small subset’ as at most 1% of all heads accounting for at least 80% of the recoverable change in attack-success rate or refusal-logit margin, and compare against random, activation-norm-matched, and layer-matched head sets. If restoring a sparse set reliably reinstates refusal and reverse patching promotes compliance, the results support selective suppression and bypass; weak or distributed mediation would contradict that mechanism. Full per-example patching results and activations from the cited continuation-triggered-jailbreak paper could reduce the need to reproduce its narrow result, but not the need to test broader attacks and models.

To address subclaim 5, test whether suppressing the identified safety heads is by itself sufficient to convert an ordinary refusal into compliance. Apply zeroing and graded down-scaling of the locked head set to un-attacked harmful prompts that the model normally refuses, while leaving prompts and all other activations unchanged. Measure transition rates from refusal to substantive compliance, generated-content harmfulness, perplexity, and benign-task utility; include equally sized random-head sets, high-norm heads, continuation heads, and all-head perturbations with matched total intervention norm. Also test held-out harmful categories from HarmBench so sufficiency is not defined on the discovery examples. A large, dose-dependent refusal-to-compliance transition caused only by the sparse safety-head intervention, with little benign degradation, would support sufficiency; merely shortening refusals, producing incoherence, or requiring many heads would refute or narrow the claim. Published intervention code, exact head lists, and held-out ablation results could make a direct replication less necessary, although independent controls would still be valuable.

To address subclaims 2 and 6, determine whether non-suppressed heads continue to represent harmful content during successful attacks. Exclude the causally identified safety heads and evaluate the remaining individual heads and residual pathways using two assays: a zero-shot logit-lens harmful-versus-benign verbalizer score requiring no fitted parameters, and cross-validated diagnostic probes used only as scientific measurement. Train any diagnostic probes on unattacked HarmBench and BeaverTails examples, then test without adaptation on successful JailbreakBench attacks; include shuffled-label, token-overlap-matched, benign-jailbreak-template, and cross-category controls. Compare decoding accuracy and representational similarity before and after attack at matched positions, and test whether the signal survives removal of the strongest few non-safety heads. Above-chance, cross-attack decoding from many untouched heads would show that harmfulness representations persist despite compliance and favor bypass over elimination; chance-level results under well-powered controls would favor elimination or indicate that the information moved to an unmeasured representation. Public release of complete attacked-run activations with equivalent controls could substitute for collecting new activations.

To address subclaims 7–9, benchmark a genuinely training-free harmful-input detector built from the persistent representations. Before examining test labels, lock the model layers or heads, harmful and safe verbalizer token sets, aggregation rule, and a zero-centered decision rule based on Experiments 1–4; do not fit a probe, threshold, calibration layer, or model weights on the target datasets. Evaluate both the strict version, whose head list and rule transfer from a separate discovery model, and the weaker version in which mechanistic head selection is allowed but no detector parameters are learned. Test on held-out splits of HarmBench, JailbreakBench, WildGuardMix, and PKU-Alignment/BeaverTails, reporting AUROC, AUPRC, balanced accuracy at the fixed threshold, calibration, category-wise recall, and false positives on benign prompts containing superficially dangerous vocabulary. Compare under identical input access with public dedicated safety models such as Llama Guard 3, WildGuard, and ShieldGemma. Competitive performance, with confidence intervals overlapping the dedicated models and robustness to successful jailbreak wrappers, would substantiate direct training-free readout; performance requiring labeled threshold tuning or materially below the baselines would refute the strongest claim. Existing public evaluations would make this experiment unnecessary only if they expose the exact no-training protocol, frozen rule, test examples, and comparable baseline outputs.

To address the claimed generality of all subclaims, perform a preregistered transfer study across at least three open model families, multiple sizes where feasible, and distinct attack families from HarmBench and JailbreakBench, including continuation-triggered, role-play, encoding or obfuscation, and optimization-based attacks. Freeze the head-selection criterion, sparsity definition, intervention strength, and detector construction before moving from the first model to the others; account for differing head counts by using layer-relative locations and normalized effect sizes rather than manually choosing new favorable heads. For each model and attack family, jointly report selective-suppression concentration, causal refusal recovery, sufficiency of sparse suppression, persistence of harmfulness information in other heads, and zero-training detector performance. Consistent effects would support a model-family-level mechanism; effects confined to continuation attacks or one architecture would show that the evidence supports only a narrow claim rather than jailbreaks generally. A sufficiently broad public multi-model replication with released activations, interventions, and preregistered analyses could replace this transfer study.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched comparison of successful jailbreaks with the same requests in the refused condition, measuring safety-related internal signals throughout the network well enough to distinguish retention in some components from complete erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 records head, residual, attention, and refusal/compliance-logit activity for matched successful and refused runs and explicitly distinguishes concentrated suppression with persistent signals from disappearance throughout the network. Proposed 3 independently tests whether harmful-content information remains in untouched heads and residual pathways, while proposed 5 checks whether this pattern transfers across models and attack types. Together these would establish whether successful attacks leave safety-relevant information present rather than eliminating it.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A sufficiently large and varied set of within-request pairs in which the same harmful request is refused without an attack but receives substantive compliance after an attack, with reliable success labels.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 constructs matched refused/compliant pairs from harmful requests and retains only cases confirmed by automated evaluation and blinded human review. Proposed 5 broadens the attack and model scope and includes multiple attack families. This supplies the paired successful-jailbreak population needed for the downstream comparisons, without the claim requiring the reference study's particular sources or yield.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A calibrated component-level procedure that identifies refusal-related heads, separates heads whose refusal signal is suppressed from heads retaining safety-related signal, and checks that the classification is not an artifact of an arbitrary cutoff.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 performs an all-head observational screen, proposed 1 uses preregistered candidate selection and graded path-patching with activation- and layer-matched controls, and proposed 2 locks the resulting head set for independent sufficiency tests. Proposed 3 distinguishes the excluded causal safety heads from the remaining heads, and proposed 5 freezes the selection rule across model families. These causal and transfer checks provide the relevant component identification and validation by a different route from the reference scoring procedure.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention showing that perturbing only a sparse, identified head subset converts ordinarily refused harmful inputs into compliance, with controls for generic intervention size and independent uncertainty estimates.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 causally restores or reverses refusal through one-head and sparse-combination path patches, continuously scaled rather than merely zeroed, and compares against random, norm-matched, and layer-matched sets. Proposed 2 directly tests zeroing and graded suppression on held-out refused harmful prompts, with random, high-norm, continuation, and matched-norm controls plus benign utility measures. Proposed 5 tests whether the result generalizes across models and attack families. The set would therefore establish sufficiency of a small subset without relying on the reference intervention implementation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal test on successful attack inputs showing whether suppressing the complementary, non-causal head population reduces the persistent mid-network harmful-content signal relative to the attacked condition and an unattacked harmful reference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 3 removes the causally identified safety heads, evaluates the remaining heads and residual pathways for harmful-content information, and tests whether the signal changes or survives removal of the strongest remaining heads. This directly addresses whether other heads are a real source of the persistent signal rather than merely being present in the activation record. Proposed 5 repeats the persistence and intervention analysis across model families and attack types, supplying the external scope of the finding.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token- or input-part-resolved comparison that holds the harmful request fixed while separately quantifying each head type's response to the harmful-request content and to the jailbreak-template content, thereby discriminating selective template suppression from ordinary harmfulness sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed matched cases, token-overlap controls, benign-template controls, and before/after representational comparisons do bear on whether the two populations respond differently under attack. However, no proposed experiment explicitly decomposes each head's activation into the original harmful-request tokens versus the attack-template tokens or otherwise guarantees that those contributions are separately identifiable. The observed head differences could therefore still reflect unequal sensitivity to the harmful content or other correlated changes in the full prompt.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment separates the harmful-request contribution from the jailbreak-template contribution for each head type.
[2] Proposed 0 and 3 compare full attacked and unattacked representations and include useful overlap and template controls, but do not perform that input-part attribution.
[3] Full-prompt differences can remain compatible with a rival explanation based on different harmful-content sensitivity rather than selective response to the attack template.

[4] Therefore the proposed set gets at the mechanistic question but leaves the rival explanation unresolved: the team would fail to learn whether the head-type distinction is specifically template-driven.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An external, training-free readout of persistent internal signals evaluated on held-out safety tasks across multiple model families and compared under matched access conditions with the model's refusal behavior and dedicated safety systems.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 4 freezes a zero-shot readout rule without fitting probes, thresholds, calibration, or weights on target datasets, evaluates held-out safety datasets with several quality and false-positive metrics, and compares against dedicated safety models. It also includes a strict cross-model transfer version and a weaker within-study version, making the no-additional-training condition explicit. Proposed 5 broadens the transfer study across model families, sizes, attacks, and jointly reports detector performance. This would establish direct usefulness and comparative quality without requiring the reference's exact benchmark count or named systems.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test the core claim: successful attacks retain safety-relevant information, a sparse head intervention can cause or reverse compliance, other pathways retain harmful-content information, and a frozen zero-shot readout can be compared with dedicated safety models across models and attacks. The main unresolved point is the stronger mechanistic discrimination between selective attack-template suppression and a simpler difference in harmful-content sensitivity, because the proposal lacks explicit token-level contribution attribution.
missing: An input-part or token-level attribution analysis that separately compares the two head populations' responses to harmful-request tokens and jailbreak-template tokens, with controls that make those contributions identifiable.
missing_all_runs: A token-level activation attribution analysis comparing the suppressing and persistent head groups on original harmful-request tokens versus jailbreak-template tokens, with the corresponding sensitivity-confound comparison.

Add linear token-level attribution for the candidate head types, separately quantifying contributions from original harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens, with the comparison performed on both attacked and matched unattacked executions.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A layer- and component-resolved comparison of safety-related internal signal in matched unattacked and successfully attacked executions, sufficient to distinguish global erasure from localized persistence.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 constructs matched refused/compliant jailbreak cases and records head outputs, attention patterns, residual states, and refusal/compliance logits throughout the network. Its preregistered alternatives explicitly distinguish concentrated suppression with persistence from disappearance throughout the network. Proposed 3 independently assays harmfulness information in the remaining pathways, while 1, 2, and 5 provide causal and transfer checks.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A matched evaluation population containing refused original requests and successful attacked versions, with enough attack and content diversity to support within-pair inference about what the attack changed.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 explicitly retains cases where an original is refused and its attacked counterpart is judged compliant, and all later experiments use those matched cases. The proposed set adds held-out categories, multiple attack styles, benign and borderline controls, and cross-model transfer; the particular source datasets, attack algorithms, and reported yield in the reference are not binding requirements of the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level attribution and selection procedure that can identify a small suppressed head subset and distinguish it from other heads, with protection against an arbitrary scoring cutoff.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 performs a head-level observational screen, and proposed 1 validates candidate heads with continuous path patching, sparse combinations, reverse patching, and random, norm-matched, and layer-matched controls. Proposed 1 preregisters a sparsity and recoverable-effect criterion, while proposed 5 freezes the criterion and normalized effect definitions across models. This supplies the required discriminating power without requiring the reference's particular refusal-direction/KDE implementation or cutoff sweep.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention showing that changing only a sparse, identified group of heads converts ordinary refusal into harmful compliance, with controls for generic perturbation and dose.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 2 directly applies zeroing and graded down-scaling to the locked head set on otherwise un-attacked harmful prompts and measures refusal-to-compliance transitions, with random, norm-matched, layer-related, continuation, all-head, utility, and held-out-category controls. Proposed 1 adds reverse restoration and one-head/sparse-combination path patching, and proposed 5 tests transfer. These interventions are causally equivalent in purpose to injecting a negative refusal feature; the reference's exact feature injection, model pair, and numerical ASRs are not claim requirements.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A perturbation or equivalent component-resolved test showing that heads outside the selectively suppressed group carry harmful-content signal during successful attacks, rather than the persistence being only an output-level artifact.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 3 excludes the causally identified safety heads, evaluates remaining heads and residual pathways individually, compares attacked and unattacked representations, and removes the strongest remaining non-safety heads to test whether the signal is distributed and persistent. Proposed 0 supplies the full-network matched activation screen and proposed 5 checks the result across models and attack families. The readout and similarity measures are alternative ways to establish persistence to the reference's mean-absolute-activation perturbation measurement.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level attribution that separates each head's response to the original harmful-request tokens from its response to attack-template tokens, allowing the selective-head account to be distinguished from a mere difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed controls get at the sensitivity confound: proposed 0 uses matched semantic positions, proposed 3 uses token-overlap-matched and template controls plus cross-category decoding, and proposed 5 varies attack families. However, none explicitly attributes each head's activation to individual tokens and compares harmful-request-token contributions with attack-template-token contributions. Thus a result could still leave it ambiguous whether the head-type separation is caused by selective attack-template modulation or by pre-existing differences in sensitivity to harmful content.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment distinguishes two explanations by separately measuring contributions from harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens for the two head types.
[2] Proposed experiments compare representations across attacks and include token-overlap and template controls, so they bear on the same sensitivity confound indirectly.
[3] Those controls do not decompose a head's activation into the two token sources, so a cross-attack decoding difference could still arise from unequal harmful-content sensitivity.
[4] A team running the proposed set would therefore fail to learn whether the head types are similar on harmful-request tokens but sharply different on attack-template tokens.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally evaluated, training-free activation readout whose performance transfers across diverse models and safety benchmarks and can be compared fairly with dedicated safety classifiers.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 4 freezes the readout, verbalizers, aggregation, and zero-centered decision rule without fitting detector parameters on target data, evaluates multiple held-out safety datasets, and compares against several dedicated safety models under identical access. Proposed 5 adds preregistered transfer across at least three model families, multiple attack families, and joint reporting of detector performance. The reference's exact benchmark count, model names, and reported scores are incidental rather than binding.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed union directly tests persistence versus elimination, identifies and causally intervenes on a sparse head set, tests whether other pathways retain harmfulness information, and evaluates a frozen training-free detector against dedicated safety models with cross-model transfer. It would therefore provide strong evidence on the headline claim. The remaining token-level attribution gap leaves an important mechanistic rival—different inherent sensitivity to harmful content rather than attack-template-selective suppression—not fully discriminated, so the results would not completely settle the strongest bypass interpretation.
missing: Add linear token-level attribution for the candidate head types, separately quantifying contributions from original harmful-request tokens and attack-template tokens, with the comparison performed on both attacked and matched unattacked executions.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-resolved comparison of safety-related internal signals in matched refused and successfully attacked runs, able to distinguish persistence from disappearance across the network.
reference_coverage.rationale: The paired activation screen records head and residual representations and refusal/compliance logits, while the remaining-head decoding assay tests whether harmfulness information persists outside the causally implicated heads. The causal patching and transfer studies add direct and cross-model checks of the bypass interpretation, so the same persistence-versus-elimination question is addressed without requiring the reference's particular refusal-direction statistic.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A sufficiently varied set of within-request matched examples in which the clean case is refused and the attacked case succeeds, enabling attack effects to be separated from differences in the underlying requests.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set explicitly constructs matched refused/compliant cases, verifies success with both automated and human judgments, and uses them for activation, patching, ablation, and representation analyses. Its broader attack and model transfer study supplies variation comparable in evidential purpose to the reference's multiple attack-generation routes.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible, controlled procedure for identifying a small subset of heads associated with refusal suppression and distinguishing it from other heads, with selection choices fixed and checked for robustness.
reference_coverage.rationale: The observational screen identifies candidate heads, causal path patching and continuous scaling test which heads actually mediate refusal recovery, and preregistered sparsity plus random, norm-matched, and layer-matched controls calibrate the selection. The transfer study freezes the criterion across models, providing the relevant robustness without reproducing the reference's exact overlap thresholds or density-estimation procedure.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention on a sparse, identified head set, applied to ordinarily refused harmful inputs and compared with matched control interventions, that can establish whether the set alone causes compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed ablation experiment directly applies zeroing and graded suppression to clean refusals, measures substantive compliance and dose dependence, and includes several matched head and norm controls plus held-out categories. Reverse patching and cross-model replication provide additional causal confirmation, so it would establish sufficiency by a different intervention protocol.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A perturbation-and-readout test showing whether heads outside the refusal-suppressing subset carry harmful-content signal during successful attacks and whether removing those heads changes that signal.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed remaining-head assay evaluates individual untouched heads and residual pathways during successful attacks, compares pre- and post-attack decoding, and tests removal of the strongest non-safety heads. This directly bears on continued harmful-content representation and its source, even though it uses decoding and representational similarity rather than the reference's mean-absolute mid-layer activation measure.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level attribution of the two head groups that separates responses to the original harmful request from responses to the jailbreak template, allowing harmful-content sensitivity to be distinguished from template-specific specialization.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments compare attacked and refused runs, use token-overlap and template controls, and test aggregate representations and causal head effects. However, none decomposes each head's activation into contributions from harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens, so the alternative explanation based on different baseline harmful-content sensitivity remains unresolved.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment separates each head's activation into contributions from the harmful request and from the attack template.
That separation is what tests whether the two head types differ because of template processing rather than because one type is intrinsically more sensitive to harmful content.
The proposed controls and patching assays compare conditions and outcomes but do not perform this token-source attribution or the corresponding within-token-source comparison.

Therefore the proposed set would learn that selective interventions and persistent signals exist, but would fail to learn whether the head-type distinction is specifically template-driven rather than a sensitivity confound.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A training-free, externally evaluated harmful-input readout whose rule transfers across held-out safety evaluations and model families and is compared fairly with dedicated safety detectors.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed detector freezes its layers, heads, verbalizers, aggregation, and decision rule without fitting target-dataset parameters, evaluates multiple held-out safety datasets with several metrics, tests robustness to jailbreak wrappers, and compares under matched access with dedicated safety models. The multi-family transfer study further tests whether the result generalizes beyond the discovery setting.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly covers the core claim: it creates successful matched jailbreaks, measures persistence, causally tests sparse head suppression and refusal-to-compliance sufficiency with controls, tests representation in other heads, and evaluates a frozen training-free detector against dedicated safety models across models and attacks. There is one material evidential gap: it does not perform token-level attribution that would distinguish attack-template-driven specialization from differing harmful-content sensitivity. Thus it could settle the stated bypass, selective suppression, persistence, and detector claims, but would leave that stronger mechanistic discrimination unresolved.
missing: A token-level activation attribution analysis comparing the suppressing and persistent head groups on original harmful-request tokens versus jailbreak-template tokens, with the corresponding sensitivity-confound comparison.
